newsitem.title: INDIA: Japan's Toyota sticks to the side lanes in India.
newsitem.headline: Japan's Toyota sticks to the side lanes in India.

text.p: Japan's largest carmaker Toyota Motor Corp's plans to make sports utility vehicles in India will make it a niche player and not a serious contender in the local automobile market, analysts said on Sunday.

The company is set to sign a $170 million joint venture with Mysore Kirloskar Ltd on Monday, 18 months after it sold its stake in its first venture in India, light commercial vehicle maker DCM Toyota Ltd, to South Korea's Daewoo Corp .

Toyota plans to make 50,000 variants of its Kijang model with 2000cc engines annually starting late 1999. It will hold a 74 percent stake in the venture located at Bidadi, near the city of Bangalore in southern India.

"Toyota has chosen a good niche. No company in India has looked at the sports utility vehicle market, and there is definitely some demand for such vehicles," Rohit Rana, automobile analyst at SocGen Crosby said.

But he said Toyota's sports utility would probably be high priced, probably in the region of 1.4 million to 1.5 million rupees ($39,200-$42,000), and late to the market, which would put it at a disadvantage against local competitors like India's largest commercial vehicle manufacturer TELCO.

"At 50,000 units a year, local content will be very low. This will keep Toyota's price high. Then, TELCO will have its own 2000cc sports utility, the Safari, out later this year at half the price at which Toyota might launch two years later," Rana said.
Rana said that TELCO had already proved how price-sensitive the market is with its Sumo jeep, which at 500,000 rupees has been well accepted by the market.
Analysts doubted Toyota would be able to sell more than 20,000 sports utilities a year.

"The market for jeeps and sports utilities currently is about 135,000 units a year, with the bulk in the rural sector and under 500,000 rupees. I don't see it growing more than 10 percent a year, putting it at about 250,000 by 2000," auto analyst Rakesh Parekh at Caspian Securities said.
He said it was highly unlikely that Toyota would be able to corner 20 percent of that market with an expensive vehicle because the appeal of sports utility vehicles in India was limited.
Parekh said Toyota's choice of the Kijang might be its undoing in India. "The Kijang is a pretty old model that's been around in Southeast Asia for some time."

He said buyers who really want to cruise around in a sports utility and are willing to pay for it will continue to import Mitsubishi Motors Corp's Pajero, the current status symbol in India, rather than buy what Toyota produces locally.
Toyota's plan to make sports utility vehicles in India capped a week of hectic activity in the automobile sector in India.
Last Monday, Fiat SpA sought Indian government permission to increase its stake to 100 percent in its $558 million joint venture with India's Premier Automobiles Ltd (PAL).
Fiat plans to make 100,000 Palios in India by late 1999 and has decided to buy out PAL's 26 percent holding in the venture.

On Tuesday, India's Eicher group called off a planned car venture with the Skoda unit of Germany's Volkswagen AG to make its Felicia model, due to sluggish demand and long gestation lags in the car business.
The Business Standard newspaper quoted Skoda's India in-charge Imran Hassan as saying the company would continue to independently pursue its plans to establish a car plant in India.
On Wednesday, TELCO announced that it would start producing a small car, tentatively christened "Indicar", by end-1998.

TELCO's chairman Ratan Tata said the firm would make 150,000 units a year to take on the Maruti 800, India's largest-selling car produced by Maruti Udyog Ltd, a joint venture between Suzuki Motor and the Indian government.
Analysts expect India's market for cars to grow to around one million units in 2000/2001 (April-March) from 345,355 in 1995/96. ($1 = 35.7 rupees)
